# Configuration reference

Tessera reads its settings from `~/Library/Application Support/Tessera/config.toml`, or from `config.toml` in the directory the `TESSERA_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable names (unset by default; for tests and side-by-side installs; it is not passed on to the shells Tessera starts, so a Tessera started from one of them reads the default directory unless it is set again). Starting Tessera writes no configuration there: without the file the defaults apply, and the file is written, with every default commented, only when the app is asked to open it for editing or a change is saved in the Settings window (a file you create yourself is picked up within a few seconds and never replaced). Saved edits of the file, and of the theme file in use under `themes/`, apply to every open window at once. Every key is optional: a missing key takes the default listed here, and a missing table takes the defaults of all its keys. Unknown keys produce a warning and are kept. A file that does not parse never stops Tessera: the error is reported, and until the file is fixed the defaults apply at launch (with `clipboard_write` off, since the file may turn it off) and the last good configuration stays in effect while running.

Defaults are written as TOML values; *unset* means the key is absent unless you set it.

## Top-level keys

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `keys` | table of string | `{}` | Key bindings: each entry maps a chord to a command, so `"cmd+shift+d" = "split_down"` (always quote the chord). An entry adds its chord to the command, ahead of its defaults: the menu item shows the first, the others stay as hidden shortcuts. An entry on another command's default chord takes it from that command; write `"cmd+t" = "unbound"` to drop a default.<br><br>A chord is zero or more modifiers and one key joined by `+`, with no spaces: modifiers `cmd` (`command`, `super`), `ctrl` (`control`), `alt` (`opt`, `option`) and `shift`, in any order and any case; the key is one lowercase character (`t`, `1`, `,`, `ö`) or a name: `escape`, `enter`, `tab`, `space`, `backspace`, `delete`, `insert`, `left`, `right`, `up`, `down`, `home`, `end`, `page_up`, `page_down`, `f1` to `f35`, `kp_0` to `kp_9`, `kp_decimal`, `kp_divide`, `kp_multiply`, `kp_subtract`, `kp_add`, `kp_enter`, `kp_equal`, and `plus`, `minus`, `equal`, `comma`, `period`, `slash`, `backslash`, `semicolon`, `apostrophe`, `grave_accent`, `left_bracket`, `right_bracket`. A shifted symbol is shorthand for Shift and its US key: `cmd+?` is `cmd+shift+/`, `cmd+plus` is `cmd+shift+=`. Uppercase keys are an error (write `shift+t`). At most 64 bytes.<br><br>A value is a command name, `send_text:<text>` (bytes written to the shell, with the escapes `\e` `\n` `\r` `\t` `\a` `\b` `\f` `\v` `\\` `\"` `\'`, `\xHH` for a raw byte and `\u{H..}` for a character; at most 4096 bytes, written as is), `unbound` (remove the chord's default) or `none` (swallow the key). Commands: `settings`, `hide`, `hide_others`, `quit`, `quit_keep_windows` (Quit and Keep Windows, or Quit and Close All Windows when macOS keeps windows on quit), `new_window`, `new_tab`, `close_tab`, `close_all_windows` (close every window, asking once), `close_window`, `clear_scrollback`, `copy`, `copy_with_formatting` (Copy as RTF and HTML too), `paste`, `paste_plain`, `select_all`, `font_bigger`, `font_smaller`, `font_reset`, `scroll_to_top`, `scroll_to_bottom`, `scroll_page_up`, `scroll_page_down`, `minimize`, `zoom`, `show_tab_bar`, `tab_previous`, `tab_next`, `move_tab_to_new_window`, `merge_all_windows`, `select_tab:1` to `select_tab:9`, `bring_all_to_front`, `help`, `about`, `show_all`, `split_right`, `split_down`, `focus_pane_left`, `focus_pane_right`, `focus_pane_up`, `focus_pane_down`, `focus_pane_previous`, `focus_pane_next`, `zoom_pane` (show the focused pane alone in its tab, or the whole layout again), `equalize_panes` (give every pane of the tab an equal share), `find`, `find_next` (the match toward older output), `find_previous` (toward newer output), `use_selection_for_find`, `copy_find_matches`, `prompt_previous` and `prompt_next` (the shell's previous or next prompt, by its OSC 133 marks; Page Up or Down when the history holds none), `select_last_output` (select the output of the last finished command), and, for features still to come, `copy_mode`.<br><br>Only chords with `cmd` appear in menus; others work in the terminal only. A malformed entry, an unknown command or a chord already bound by an earlier entry (an `unbound` entry too) is ignored with a warning (the first entry not ignored for another reason wins); at most 512 entries are read.<br><br>The Settings window's Keys pane writes a new chord in the canonical form (`cmd+ctrl+alt+shift+key`). An entry you write by hand in another form (modifiers in another order, an alias such as `opt`, a shifted symbol such as `cmd+?`) is found by the chord it binds: replacing or recording again changes that entry under its own key, so the file keeps one entry per chord, and one that sends text or is `none` shows as a conflict. When the file holds the chord in two spellings, the pane changes the one that took effect. Restore Defaults keeps entries that send text or are `none` (#355). |

## `[appearance]`

Default appearance; profiles may override.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `app_appearance` | one of `"dark"`, `"light"`, `"system"` | `"dark"` | Whether Tessera's own windows, context menus and Settings are drawn dark, light or as the system's appearance (System Settings > Appearance) says: `"dark"`, `"light"` or `"system"`, exactly as written here. Only the window's chrome follows it: the terminal's colours stay the theme's. Applies to open windows when the file changes. Any other value is reported with a warning and `"dark"` is used. Set it here only: in a profile's `appearance` it is ignored with a warning, since it applies to the whole app. |
| `blur` | boolean | `false` | Background blur behind each pane whose background is translucent (`opacity` below 1.0, or a theme background with alpha). The title bar and tab bar of a translucent window are always blurred, whatever this says. Off while the system's Reduce Transparency setting is on. |
| `blur_radius` | integer | `48` | How strongly a translucent window blurs what is behind it, from 0 to 64 (`Appearance::MAX_BLUR_RADIUS`); default 48. 0 is no blur at all, under the title bar and tab bar too; 1 to 64 blurs the title bar and tab bar of a translucent window and each translucent pane that asks for `blur`, inside the window's rounded corners. macOS has no blur of a chosen radius behind a window, so the value is the strength of the system's blur: 64 is all of it, 32 half of it over the unblurred desktop. Until 0.3.0, 0 (then the default) kept the system's blur behind each pane that asked for `blur`: the line `blur_radius = 0` the 0.2.0 and 0.2.1 templates wrote, untouched under their comment ("No effect in 0.2.0 ..."), still reads as the default (the file is not rewritten), and setting the key in Settings drops that comment; any other 0 turns the blur off. A value above 64 is lowered to 64 with a warning; a negative or fractional one (`-1`, `20.0`) makes the file invalid, as for `scrollback_lines`. It applies to open windows when the file changes. Set it here only: in a profile's `appearance` it is ignored with a warning, since the window, not the session, is blurred. |
| `cursor_blink` | boolean | `false` | Whether the cursor blinks, unless a program says otherwise (as for `cursor_shape`). tmux and vim turn blinking off on their own (`CSI ? 12 l`), so inside a running tmux a blinking cursor stays off until this is next changed. Changing it applies to open tabs, also where a program turned blinking on or off, but a program still running, such as tmux, may turn it off again. Recorded only for now: the cursor is drawn steady. A value that is not `true` or `false` is reported with a warning and the default is used. |
| `cursor_shape` | one of `"block"`, `"underline"`, `"beam"` | `"block"` | The cursor's shape: `"block"`, `"underline"` or `"beam"` (a vertical bar), exactly as written here. A program may change it (DECSCUSR, `CSI Ps SP q`, as vim and fish do); it returns to this one when the program asks for the default or resets the terminal. Any other value is reported with a warning and the default is used. |
| `dim_inactive_panes` | float | `0.0` | How much to darken the panes of a split tab that do not have the keyboard focus, from 0.0 (off) to 0.8, drawn as a black overlay of that opacity. A tab with one pane is never dimmed. A value outside the range is clamped (not a number means 0.0) with a warning. Applies to open windows when the file changes. Set it here only: in a profile's `appearance` it is ignored with a warning, since the window, not the session, draws it. |
| `font_family` | string | `"Menlo"` | Font family. |
| `font_size` | float | `13.0` | Font size in points, clamped on load to `4.0`..=`512.0`. |
| `opacity` | float | `1.0` | Background opacity, 0.0..=1.0. A window is translucent while any pane of its tab is. While the window is translucent its title bar and tab bar are always blurred, whatever `blur` says, and tinted with the theme's background at this opacity. The system's Reduce Transparency setting draws every session opaque. |
| `theme` | string | `"Tessera Dark"` | Colour theme, by name. Looked up first among the `*.toml` files in `themes/` next to this file (by file stem, then by the `name` key inside each file), then among the bundled themes: Tessera Dark, Tessera Light, Solarized Dark, Solarized Light, Dracula, Nord, Gruvbox Dark, One Dark, Tokyo Night and Catppuccin Mocha. Names match ignoring case, and any run of characters other than letters and digits counts as one separator, with `+` read as the word `plus`: `solarized-dark` and `SOLARIZED DARK` are Solarized Dark, `Dracula+` is `dracula-plus`, not Dracula, but `solarizeddark` is not Solarized Dark. A user file shadows a bundled theme of the same name. Unicode is not normalised, so an accented name matches only when typed in the same form (precomposed or combining) as the theme's. An unknown name falls back to Tessera Dark with a warning. |

## `[general]`

Application-wide settings.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `confirm_close` | boolean | `true` | Confirm before closing a window with running jobs. |
| `default_profile` | string | `"Default"` | The profile (a `[[profiles]]` entry or a file in `profiles/`) new tabs, windows and panes use when none is chosen (a pane split off another uses that pane's). When no profile has this name, the built-in one is used: `[appearance]` and the login shell (with a warning, unless the name is `"Default"`). |
| `remote_indicator` | one of `"title"`, `"off"` | `"title"` | How a tab whose shell runs on another machine is marked: `"title"` puts `⇢ <host>: ` before its title, the host taken from the shell's working-directory report (OSC 7), or `⇢ ssh` when `ssh` runs with no such report; `"off"` shows titles unchanged. Applies to open tabs when the file changes. Any other value is reported with a warning and `"title"` is used. |

## `[notifications]`

System notifications when a long command finishes (ADR 0048).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `command_finished` | one of `"unfocused"`, `"off"` | `"off"` | When a command that ran at least `command_finished_after` seconds finishes, `"unfocused"` posts a system notification and marks its tab, unless its pane has the keyboard (the app is active, its window is key, its tab selected and the pane focused); `"off"` does neither. Needs shell integration's prompt marks (OSC 133). The first notification asks macOS for permission. At most 10 are posted a minute; the tab is marked all the same. Set here only: no profile changes it. Any other value is reported with a warning and `"off"` is used. |
| `command_finished_after` | integer | `10` | How long a command must run, in whole seconds (1 to 86400), before its finish notifies. A value outside the range is clamped to it with a warning. Set here only: no profile changes it. |

## `[plugins]`

Plugin enablement, keyed by plugin id.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | array of string | `[]` | Plugin ids that are enabled, from the plugins built into this version (`dev.tessera.hello`). Applies when the file changes: a newly listed plugin is activated, a removed one deactivated. A plugin that declares a capability this version does not grant is refused, one that panics or fails to start is marked failed until it is removed and listed again. At most 64 ids of at most 128 bytes are read; a longer, unknown or extra id is ignored with a warning. |

## `[[profiles]]`

Named profiles.

A profile can also live in a file of its own: `profiles/<name>.toml` next to `config.toml` holds the keys of one `[[profiles]]` entry, written at the top level of the file (`command = "/bin/zsh"`, then `[appearance]`), and its `name` defaults to the file name without `.toml`. The profiles of the files follow the `[[profiles]]` entries, sorted by file name (byte order, so `B.toml` before `a.toml`); of two profiles with one name, the first is used and the second is reported with a warning, and `default_profile` may name either. At most 256 profiles are used in all and at most 256 files are read (the first by name; the rest are reported with one warning). A file larger than 64 KiB, or one that is not UTF-8 or TOML or has a value of the wrong type, is skipped with a warning naming it; files not ending in `.toml`, hidden files and anything that is not a file are ignored, and symbolic links are followed. A profile file saved, added or removed applies at once, as an edit of `config.toml` does, with one exception: a file saved in place (not by an editor that writes a new file and renames it over the old one) after the first 32 by name applies with the next change in `profiles/`. The Settings window edits `config.toml` only: it shows the profiles of the files but does not change them (edit the file).

An array of tables: write one `[[profiles]]` block per entry. Default: `[]`.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `appearance` | table, optional | *unset* | Appearance for this profile's sessions: each key set here replaces the one in `[appearance]`, each key left out follows `[appearance]` (also when it changes). In 0.1.0 a key left out here was reset to its built-in default instead (a profile that set only `font_size` also reset `theme`, `opacity` and the cursor). `dim_inactive_panes`, `blur_radius` and `app_appearance` cannot be set here (the window or the app draws them): they are ignored with a warning. See [`[profiles.appearance]`](#profilesappearance). |
| `command` | string, optional | *unset* | Command to run instead of the login shell: one program name or path runs directly (`"/opt/homebrew/bin/fish"`), anything with a space runs through `/bin/sh -c` (`"ssh build-box"`). Unset means the login shell. A command that cannot be started (the program does not exist or is not executable, or the command is longer than the system lets a program's arguments be) starts your login shell in your home directory instead, with a line in the new session saying so. A command with a space is started by `/bin/sh`, which always exists: when the program it names is missing, the shell reports it in the session and exits, with no fallback. A command with a NUL character is ignored with a warning, as if unset. |
| `name` | string | `"Default"` | Display name, shown in the menus. Should be unique: of two profiles with one name, the first is used and the second is reported with a warning. A NUL character in it is replaced with U+FFFD, with a warning. |
| `working_directory` | string, optional | *unset* | Starting directory; `~` at the start is your home directory. A directory that does not exist falls back to your home directory with a warning; one that exists but cannot be entered, or is on a volume that gives no answer within 5 s, starts your login shell in your home directory, with a line in the new session saying so. Used only when the session is not given a directory of its own; unset means your home directory. One with a NUL character is ignored with a warning, as if unset. |

### `[profiles.appearance]`

Appearance for this profile's sessions: each key set here replaces the one in `[appearance]`, each key left out follows `[appearance]` (also when it changes). In 0.1.0 a key left out here was reset to its built-in default instead (a profile that set only `font_size` also reset `theme`, `opacity` and the cursor). `dim_inactive_panes`, `blur_radius` and `app_appearance` cannot be set here (the window or the app draws them): they are ignored with a warning.

Optional table; *unset* by default. It belongs to the `[[profiles]]` entry it follows.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `blur` | boolean, optional | *unset* | Background blur behind each of this profile's panes whose background is translucent (`opacity` below 1.0, or a theme background with alpha). The title bar and tab bar of a translucent window are always blurred, whatever this says. |
| `cursor_blink` | boolean, optional | *unset* | Whether the cursor blinks, as for `[appearance] cursor_blink`. A value that is not `true` or `false` is reported with a warning and `[appearance]`'s value is used. |
| `cursor_shape` | one of `"block"`, `"underline"`, `"beam"` | *unset* | The cursor's shape, `"block"`, `"underline"` or `"beam"`, as for `[appearance] cursor_shape`. Any other value is reported with a warning and `[appearance]`'s shape is used. |
| `font_family` | string, optional | *unset* | Font family. Not honoured per profile yet: the font is shared by every session, so only `[appearance] font_family` changes it. |
| `font_size` | float, optional | *unset* | Font size in points, clamped on load as for `[appearance] font_size`. A value that is not a finite number (`nan`, `inf`) is ignored with a warning, so `[appearance]`'s applies. |
| `opacity` | float, optional | *unset* | Background opacity of this profile's sessions, 0.0..=1.0. A window is translucent while any pane of its tab is, and stays opaque only while every one is; an opaque session still draws its own opaque background. While the window is translucent its title bar and tab bar are always blurred, whatever `blur` says. The system's Reduce Transparency setting draws every session opaque. A value that is not a finite number is ignored with a warning, so `[appearance]`'s applies. |
| `theme` | string, optional | *unset* | Colour theme, by name, looked up as for `[appearance] theme`. |

## `[selection]`

Smart selection on a double-click, and Copy's trailing blanks.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `smart_rules` | array of tables | *unset* | The rules a double-click tries before selecting the word: each a table with a `regex` (the Rust `regex` crate's syntax: no look-around, no back-references) and a `precision` (`"very_low"`, `"low"`, `"normal"`, `"high"` or `"very_high"`). Of the matches that cover the clicked character, the one with the highest precision weight times length wins (one level is worth a thousand times the length; then the more precise, the longer, the earlier one, the earlier rule); with none, the word is selected. Matching looks at most 8192 characters and 32 KiB around the click along the logical line (half before it); where the line goes on past an edge of that window, a match starting or ending in the unbroken run of non-blank characters at that edge is not taken.<br><br>Unset, the built-in rules apply: file paths, `http`, `https`, `ssh`, `telnet` and `mailto` URLs (a URL loses trailing punctuation and unbalanced closing brackets), email addresses, double-quoted strings, C++ `a::b` and dotted `a.b.c` names, Objective-C selectors, git hashes, and IPv4 and IPv6 addresses (ADR 0042 lists their patterns). A list replaces them all. At most 64 rules are read; a rule whose pattern is longer than 1024 bytes, does not compile, is too complex or matches the empty string is ignored with a warning. A rule with a Unicode word boundary whose program is very large, such as `\b\w{20}`, matches on lines that are all ASCII but selects nothing on a line with other characters, with one warning, logged by the first double-click after the rules load. Like every rule, it can also select nothing on an ASCII line when its search would need more memory than a rule may keep. A rule that is a large set of exact strings (more than about 64) may skip the literal search shortcut to stay within that memory; its matches are the same. See [`[[selection.smart_rules]]`](#selectionsmart_rules). |
| `trim_trailing_whitespace` | boolean | `true` | Whether Copy drops the blanks after the last text of each line (and blank lines at the end of the selection). Off, each row keeps its blanks up to the selection's end (a whole row for every row but the last), up to the last row with text. |

### `[[selection.smart_rules]]`

The rules a double-click tries before selecting the word: each a table with a `regex` (the Rust `regex` crate's syntax: no look-around, no back-references) and a `precision` (`"very_low"`, `"low"`, `"normal"`, `"high"` or `"very_high"`). Of the matches that cover the clicked character, the one with the highest precision weight times length wins (one level is worth a thousand times the length; then the more precise, the longer, the earlier one, the earlier rule); with none, the word is selected. Matching looks at most 8192 characters and 32 KiB around the click along the logical line (half before it); where the line goes on past an edge of that window, a match starting or ending in the unbroken run of non-blank characters at that edge is not taken.

Unset, the built-in rules apply: file paths, `http`, `https`, `ssh`, `telnet` and `mailto` URLs (a URL loses trailing punctuation and unbalanced closing brackets), email addresses, double-quoted strings, C++ `a::b` and dotted `a.b.c` names, Objective-C selectors, git hashes, and IPv4 and IPv6 addresses (ADR 0042 lists their patterns). A list replaces them all. At most 64 rules are read; a rule whose pattern is longer than 1024 bytes, does not compile, is too complex or matches the empty string is ignored with a warning. A rule with a Unicode word boundary whose program is very large, such as `\b\w{20}`, matches on lines that are all ASCII but selects nothing on a line with other characters, with one warning, logged by the first double-click after the rules load. Like every rule, it can also select nothing on an ASCII line when its search would need more memory than a rule may keep. A rule that is a large set of exact strings (more than about 64) may skip the literal search shortcut to stay within that memory; its matches are the same.

An array of tables: write one `[[selection.smart_rules]]` block per entry.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `precision` | one of `"very_low"`, `"low"`, `"normal"`, `"high"`, `"very_high"` | `"normal"` | How much a match counts: `"very_low"`, `"low"`, `"normal"`, `"high"` or `"very_high"`; a match scores the precision's weight times its length, one level being worth a thousand times the length. |
| `regex` | string | `""` | The regular expression, in the `regex` crate's syntax (no look-around, no back-references): at most 1024 bytes, and it must not match the empty string. |

## `[terminal]`

Terminal emulation limits and shell integration.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `clipboard_write` | boolean | `true` | Whether programs may write the clipboard (OSC 52, as tmux and Neovim do over `ssh`): up to 1 MiB of text per write. Programs can never read the clipboard. A value that is not `true` or `false` is reported with a warning and counts as `false`: writes are refused until it is fixed. When Tessera starts with a `config.toml` that does not load at all (a syntax error anywhere in it, such as `clipboard_write = off` without quotes, a duplicate key, a file that is not UTF-8, a `config.toml` symlink whose target is missing, or a configuration directory that is such a symlink, as when a dotfiles volume is not mounted), writes are refused as well until the file is fixed (or the directory appears, also when the link is above the configuration directory), while the other defaults apply; emptying the file (or leaving only a byte order mark) does not turn them back on (a save that truncates first leaves it empty for a moment; one gap: an appeared directory opened with ⌘, within two seconds, before Tessera has noticed it, does), only a version of it with something in it that loads. Applies to every session at once when changed. |
| `paste_guard` | one of `"unbracketed"`, `"always"`, `"off"` | `"unbracketed"` | When a paste asks first, on a sheet that shows the text with its control characters escaped and its line count: `"unbracketed"` asks when the text holds a line break and the program has not turned on bracketed paste (DECSET 2004), so each line would run as a command, or when it holds control characters (C0 other than tab, line feed and carriage return, DEL or C1, which the paste removes); `"always"` asks before every paste; `"off"` never asks. Cancel is the default button, so a Return typed after ⌘V does not paste. Applies to the next paste when changed. |
| `scrollback_lines` | integer | `10000` | Maximum number of scrollback lines kept per pane. Applies to sessions started after a change; running sessions keep the size they started with. Large values cost time on every width change: resizing a window re-wraps the whole history while the terminal is locked, about 0.2 ms per 1,000 lines (1-4 ms at 10,000 lines, 14-41 ms at 100,000), so at the 10,000,000 limit a full history takes about 18 GB of memory and each resize stalls the pane for 2-4 seconds. |
| `shell_integration` | one of `"auto"`, `"off"` | `"auto"` | Shell integration for zsh, bash and fish: `"auto"` makes the shells Tessera starts load its scripts, which mark prompts and commands and report the working directory; `"off"` starts them unchanged. A session started with `TESSERA_SHELL_INTEGRATION` in its environment is never changed. |
